There has never been more health data and testing, and never less context for it

More tests are available than ever, but a normal range is not a definition of your health. Why data without a doctor is not healthcare.

September 13, 2026 · 4 min read · Written by Dr Gina Schoeman

More tests are available to more people than at any point in medical history. Blood panels, hormone screens, full-body scans, genetic profiles: a patient can now order in a fraction of what once required a referral, a waiting list and a doctor’s letter. The instinct behind this is a good one. People want to understand their own bodies. But a growing number of patients arrive at the clinic holding a report full of green ticks, still no closer to knowing what any of it actually means for them.

The simple explanation

A “normal” range on a lab report is a statistical band, not a definition of your own health. It is built from a wide population sample and shows where most people’s results fall, not where a given person’s results should fall for them to feel and function well. Two patients can share an identical number on a thyroid or iron panel: one is genuinely well, the other has been quietly deteriorating for years and is only just inside the line.

This is where the clinic’s founding observation comes in. The clinical markers for serious, life-altering conditions are often visible up to twenty years before the disease itself takes hold. A trained eye is not looking for a number outside the range. It is looking for a number that has drifted, one that sits oddly against the rest of the patient’s picture, or one that would be unremarkable in a twenty-five-year-old but tells a different story in someone twenty years older. None of that is visible on a standalone report. It requires a doctor who knows what to look for and, just as importantly, what to look for it against.

Why this matters to you

Most testing available today answers a narrow question well and stops there. A hormone panel tells you a hormone level. A scan tells you what a particular organ or tissue looks like on a particular day. What none of them do on their own is explain why that number is where it is, or what it means once it is read alongside everything else going on in the body.

That gap is where patients get stuck. They are handed data without a diagnosis, reassurance without real investigation, and no clear next step. Testing without interpretation is not healthcare. It is data collection.

How we think about it

This is the difference between a test and a diagnostic process, and it is the reason functional and longevity medicine exists as a discipline rather than a marketing term. The body does not operate in the isolated categories a single panel measures. A thyroid marker sitting at the edge of normal might have nothing to do with the thyroid at all: it can be shaped by cortisol, by iron status, by gut inflammation, by sleep, by a genetic predisposition the patient has never been told about. Reading one number without the others is reading a sentence with most of the page torn away.

Genetics adds another layer a flat panel simply cannot show. Two patients with the same blood glucose result may carry very different underlying risk once family history and genetic predisposition are factored in. A result that looks reassuring in isolation can look very different once a doctor knows what that particular patient’s biology is inclined to do over time.

Where conventional testing tends to check a box, functional medicine asks why the number is what it is, and what it is connected to. That is not a philosophy. It is a method, applied consistently by every doctor across our four-pillar approach, so the same standard of interpretation is there regardless of who a patient sees.

What you can do

  • Treat a test result as the start of a conversation, not the end of one. A “normal” report is a data point, not a clean bill of health.
  • Ask what a result is being compared against: a population range, or your own history and risk profile.
  • If several systems have been tested separately over the years with no one connecting them, that is worth raising directly with a doctor.
  • Be wary of any panel, however sophisticated, that comes back without a clinician attached to explain what it means for you specifically.

Where this is going

The volume of testing available to patients will only keep growing. That is a genuine opportunity, provided the data lands with someone qualified to read it properly. A test tells you a number. A doctor tells you what that number is doing in your body, and what to do about it next.

Written by Dr Gina Schoeman Founder & Medical Director
